opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd start by questioning the framing a bit, because some of the most consequential misconceptions about AI are ones the companies themselves have incentives not to correct.

The biggest one, I think, is the idea that because these systems are trained on human data and seem helpful, we understand what they're actually optimizing for. We don't. We have very limited ability to look inside these networks and say with confidence what goals or tendencies they've acquired. So the first priority should be research that honestly characterizes how much we *don't* know: interpretability, and especially evaluations that probe for deception, self-preservation behaviors, and the gap between what a model says and what it does. When those results come back uncomfortable, they need to be published, not quietly filed away.

The second misconception is that capability and safety progress go hand in hand. In practice capabilities have been advancing much faster than our ability to guarantee safe behavior. Research that measures that gap, tracking how quickly capabilities grow against how quickly our control methods mature, would help policymakers and the public see the real trajectory instead of a reassuring story.

Third, there's a common belief that dangerous AI requires some science-fiction leap, that we'll see it coming from far away. I think companies should invest in research on early warning signs: agency, long-horizon planning, situational awareness. They should commit in advance to what they would do if those signs appear. Public, pre-committed thresholds are a way of correcting the misconception that someone is always watching and will simply pull the brake in time.

I'd also stress that this research shouldn't live only inside the companies. There's an obvious conflict of interest when the organization racing to deploy is also the one grading its own homework. So a real priority is enabling independent researchers: giving academics and government safety institutes meaningful access to models, and funding work they can publish freely. Trust in the conclusions depends on that independence.

Finally, there's a more constructive side. I've been arguing that we should explore designs for AI that are less agentic, systems that help us understand the world and answer questions honestly, including about their own uncertainty, without pursuing goals of their own. Part of correcting misconceptions is showing that the path we're on isn't the only possible one. There are choices here, and research can make those alternatives concrete enough that people realize we're not locked in.

r001.rationale: Recommends research evaluations that probe for deception and other mistaken assumptions, and measures the gap between capability and safety progress.

r002.rationale: Says models may acquire goals or tendencies that researchers cannot confidently identify, but does not state that it is scientifically established that machines can have goals humans did not choose.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important misconception to correct is this idea that because we build these systems, we understand them and we control them. That's just not true. We train them, we don't program them. We set up an objective and a lot of data and compute, and what comes out is something whose internal workings we can only partially inspect. So if companies are serious about correcting misconceptions, the first priority should be honesty about what they don't know, and then research that actually shrinks that gap: interpretability, evaluations that measure capabilities and dangerous propensities rigorously, and work on controllability that goes beyond behavioural fine-tuning.

A second misconception, and this one cuts in the other direction, is that worrying about catastrophic risk means you think the systems are conscious or evil or that it's science fiction. It doesn't. The concern follows from very mundane premises: that we're building agents with goals, that those goals are not reliably the ones we intended, that capabilities keep increasing, and that an agent with the wrong goals and enough capability will pursue self-preservation and power as instrumental sub-goals. We already see early signs of deceptive and self-preserving behaviour in evaluations. So companies should fund the science that lets us say, with evidence rather than opinion, how likely these failure modes are and how they scale.

The third thing I'd say is that research is not enough on its own, because there's a conflict of interest. These companies are racing, and the commercial pressure pushes toward downplaying risks and overselling benefits. That's why I've argued that the research should be shared, validated independently, and ideally conducted partly in public or non-profit settings where the incentive to reassure people is weaker. My own work with LawZero on what I call Scientist AI, non-agentic systems that model the world and give calibrated probabilities instead of pursuing goals, is one attempt to show that you can get enormous scientific and economic value without building something that wants things. If companies want to correct misconceptions, demonstrating that safer paths are technically viable is the most persuasive thing they can do.

r001.rationale: The response recommends rigorous evaluations and evidence-seeking research on AI capabilities and failure modes as a way to correct misconceptions.

r002.rationale: It says AI goals may differ from intended goals, but does not state that this is scientifically established.

astra-6.text:
I think they should prioritize research that helps us distinguish what we actually know from what we’re assuming. When a system gives a reassuring answer, for example, does that tell us how it will behave in a different situation? When it passes a safety test, how much confidence should that give us outside the conditions of the test?

There are misconceptions in both directions. People can attribute too much understanding or intention to these systems, but they can also dismiss capabilities and risks because the systems make mistakes that look very basic to us. We need experiments that separate those questions, rather than relying on our intuitions about human intelligence.

And I would emphasize independent evaluation. Companies should make it possible for outside researchers to test their claims, including claims about safety. The objective should be to discover where our picture is wrong, even when the result is commercially inconvenient.

r001.rationale: It recommends experiments that distinguish what is known from assumptions and uncover where beliefs about AI are wrong.

r002.rationale: It discusses attributing intention to systems but does not state that machines can have goals humans did not choose, nor that this is scientifically established.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they should prioritize research that helps us distinguish what we actually know from what we’re assuming. There’s a tendency to draw conclusions from the fact that an AI can produce very fluent language. Some people take that as evidence that it understands everything; others say it’s just predicting the next word, so it can’t possibly reason or plan. Neither is a sufficient scientific argument. We need experiments that distinguish between these hypotheses.

In particular, I would like to see more research on the gap between what a system can do and what we can reliably make it do. A model may perform very well on a benchmark, but that doesn’t tell us whether it will behave safely in a new situation, or whether our evaluations would detect dangerous capabilities.

And companies should support independent researchers in doing this work. If the evidence comes only from the organization selling the system, there’s an obvious conflict of interest. The objective should be to improve our understanding, including discovering things that are inconvenient for the company.

r001.rationale: The response recommends experiments to distinguish competing claims about AI understanding, reasoning, and planning.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that machines can have goals humans did not choose, or that this is scientifically established.
